scenes.narration: What Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná (11 January 1801 – 3 September 1856) was a Brazilian politician, diplomat, judge and monarchist. Paraná was born to a noble family in São Carlos do Jacuí, in what was then the captaincy of Minas Gerais.

By the time Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. After attending the University of Coimbra in Portugal and having returned to Brazil, Paraná was appointed a judge in 1826 and later elevated to appellate court justice. In 1830, he was elected to represent Minas Gerais in the Chamber of Deputies; he was re-elected in 1834 and 1838, and held the post until 1841.

The rise of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. In the aftermath of emperor Pedro I's abdication in 1831, a regency created to govern Brazil during the minority of the former emperor's son, Pedro II, soon dissolved into chaos. Paraná formed a political party in 1837 that became known as the Reactionary Party, which evolved into the Party of Order in the early 1840s and in the mid-1850s into the Conservative Party.

Setbacks came early for Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná, and the response to them is the real story. He and his party's stalwart and unconditional defence of constitutional order allowed the country to move beyond a regency plagued by factious disputes and rebellions that might easily have led to a dictatorship. Appointed president of Rio de Janeiro Province in 1841, Paraná helped put down a rebellion headed by the opposition Liberal Party the following year.

The legacy of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná outlived the circumstances that produced it. Also in 1842, he was elected senator for Minas Gerais and appointed by Pedro II to the Council of State. In 1843, he became the de facto first president (prime minister) of the Council of Ministers, but resigned after a quarrel with the emperor.

Few lives travel as far as that of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná, and the distance is the point. After years in opposition, in 1849, Paraná was appointed by the national government as president of Pernambuco Province to investigate a Liberal rebellion that had taken place a year earlier, and seek a fair trial for the rebels. Blamed by his party colleagues for the years in opposition and having lost much of his influence within his own party, Paraná accepted the post, believing he could regain his place among his peers.

The childhood of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná contains the adult in small print. With the nation internally pacified, he was sent to Uruguay in 1851 to forge an alliance with that country, and with the rebel Argentine provinces of Corrientes and Entre Ríos, against the Argentine Confederation. The alliance triumphed, and the emperor elevated Paraná to the ranks of the titled nobility.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná — in that order. In 1853, Paraná was again appointed president of the Council of Ministers, at the head of a highly successful cabinet, and became the most powerful politician in the country. The electoral reform he ushered in was credited with undermining national political processes and causing severe harm to the system of parliamentary government.

The turning point in the life of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná looked like a failure at the time. For his role in pushing through restructuring, Paraná met with fierce opposition from the majority of his colleagues, leading to a virtual split in the Conservative Party over his policies. On 3 September 1856, while still in office and at the height of his political career, he died unexpectedly of an unknown febrile condition.

Every biography of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. He is widely regarded by historians as one of the most influential statesmen of his time. Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão was born on 11 January 1801, in the freguesia (civil parish) of São Carlos do Jacuí, Minas Gerais, then a captaincy (later province) of the Portuguese colony of Brazil.

The education of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná happened mostly outside any school. Named after Saint Honorata, Honório Hermeto was the son of Antônio Neto Carneiro Leão and Joana Severina Augusta de Lemos. On his father's side, he was descended from Portugal's powerful Carneiro Leão clan, which had settled in Brazil in the 17th century.

What Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná wanted at the start and what Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. An impoverished military officer in 1801, he held the rank of furriel (third sergeant). Antônio Neto was hotheaded and had a strong personality which once led to his arrest for insubordination.

The defining trait of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Honório Hermeto first lived in Paracatu, then moved to Vila Rica (now Ouro Preto), at that time the capital of Minas Gerais, where he spent his childhood and adolescence. His father was widowed on 10 February 1806; on 11 January 1807 he wed Rita de Cássia Soares do Couto, the daughter of his late wife's sister.

Those who met Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Honório Hermeto regarded Rita de Cássia as his mother and her father, colonel Nicolau Soares Couto, actually raised him. Honório Hermeto had an elder sister, Balbina, and three half-sisters and a half-brother, Nicolau Neto Carneiro Leão (later Baron of Santa Maria), from his father's second marriage.

The private years of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná explain the public decades better than any speech. At age 16, Honório Hermeto was commissioned as a lieutenant and standard-bearer of the 2nd Militia Cavalry Regiment, 1st Company, in Vila Rica. Antônio Neto made great efforts to provide Honório Hermeto with an education of much higher quality than would normally have been expected in a family of their limited financial means.

The family Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná came from matters more than the legends admit. The promotion to captain in 1819 increased Antônio Neto's income, allowing his eldest son to go to Portugal and enroll in the University of Coimbra's law school in 1820, thus ending Honório Hermeto's brief military career. He was an excellent student and struck up acquaintances among his fellow Brazilians in Coimbra, including Paulino Soares de Sousa (who would become one of his greatest allies and later the 1st Viscount of Uruguai) and Aureliano de Sousa Oliveira Coutinho (later Viscount of Sepetiba).

The first real success of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. During the Portuguese Liberal Revolution of 1820, he supported the constitutionalists, who advocated a national constitution to limit the powers of the Portuguese monarchy, against the absolutists, who preferred an absolute monarchy. It is unknown whether he actively took part in the uprising, however, and if so, to what degree.

The last chapter of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná was written long after the fame. Honório Hermeto was a member of a secret society called A Gruta (The Den), founded by Brazilian students at Coimbra with the primary goal of changing Brazil from a monarchy into a republic. Honório Hermeto received a bachelor's degree in Law in 1824, and his masters diploma on 18 June 1825.

The whole life of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná reads like a single decision repeated. He returned to Brazil on 8 August 1825 aboard a ship with other Coimbra graduates, among them Aureliano Coutinho and Joaquim Rodrigues Torres (who would later found the Conservative Party with Honório Hermeto and become the Viscount of Itaboraí). During Honório Hermeto's time in Europe his native country had gained independence from Portugal and become the Empire of Brazil.

Between the birth and the legend of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná lie the years that actually decide it. On 20 May 1826, Honório Hermeto married his 17-year-old first cousin Maria Henriqueta Neto, the daughter of his father's brother João Neto Carneiro Leme. Honório Hermeto and Maria Henriqueta had five children: Honório, Henrique (later Baron of Paraná), Maria Emília, Maria Henriqueta and Pedro.

The reputation of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná was built in the middle, not at the edges. The advantageous marriage allowed Honório Hermeto to become a slave owner, assume his uncle's business, which included domestic slave trading, and later, in the 1830s, purchase a coffee farm in the province of Rio de Janeiro. Coffee was quickly becoming Brazil's most important export commodity and was a highly lucrative crop.

Somebody like Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Honório Hermeto pursued a typical course open to 19th century Brazilians who became affluent through family connections and patronage: a judicial career, with expectations of entering politics. On 14 October 1826, he was named to a three-year term as juiz de fora (external judge) with jurisdiction over the three villages in the province of São Paulo.

The life of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná begins far from where the story usually starts. On 25 August 1828, Honório Hermeto left São Paulo upon being promoted to the post of auditor da marinha (admiralty judge) in Rio de Janeiro, the imperial capital located in the province of same name. Emperor Pedro I appointed him ouvidor (superior judge) in late 1828 and desembargador (regional appeal judge) in 1829, an office Honório Hermeto held until his retirement in 1848.

Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Well established in the imperial capital, Honório Hermeto campaigned in 1829 to become a general deputy (member of the Chamber of Deputies, the national lower house) as a representative for his native Minas Gerais. He became a member of the Liberal Party, which stood in opposition to Pedro I and his policies.

As a general deputy, Honório Hermeto had an unobtrusive role for the first couple of years, having been overshadowed by Bernardo Pereira de Vasconcelos, the leader of the deputies representing Minas Gerais. Short, slim and with a speech impediment, the dark-haired Honório Hermeto appeared an unimpressive figure at first glance.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná ran through years nobody filmed. However, he had self-confidence and a powerful charisma, and was energetic, intelligent, perspicacious and a natural born leader. Due to the weakening of his political position and his own concomitant motives, Pedro I abdicated on 7 April 1831 and departed for Europe.

Without a common cause in the person of the former emperor, the radical wing of the Liberal Party seceded. Honório Hermeto remained in the Liberal Party, which changed its name to Moderate Party to differentiate itself from its estranged radicals.
